Combined with the intrusion-focused threat items, it weakens coherence with a natural-disaster trauma profile.

vignette:
Mark, a 45-year-old military medic, had always prided himself on his resilience. However, since the devastating earthquake that struck his small coastal town two years ago, his sense of self had been irrevocably altered. The ground had trembled violently, swallowing homes and lives in a matter of moments. Mark had been on duty, tending to the injured, but even as he worked tirelessly to save others, he couldn't shake the feeling that he was failing. The cacophony of screams and the relentless roar of collapsing structures haunted him. He vividly remembered the moment he found a neighbor's lifeless body, a sight that would replay in his mind with a terror that felt as fresh as the day it happened. Each recollection would send him spiraling into a whirlpool of emotions, making him feel overwhelmed and forcing him to push the memories aside, struggling to piece together the chaotic sequence of events that had led to such devastation.

Since that day, Mark had been living in a state of constant alertness. It was as if the earthquake had flipped a switch in his mind, leaving him hypervigilant and on edge. Even the slightest unexpected sound-a door slamming, a car backfiring-would send his heart racing. This constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof Mark had that his life had changed beyond repair, reinforcing his belief that he was no longer the resilient person he once was. Feeling this perpetual threat led him to accept a painful truth: that he was now someone who could not feel safe, and this realization fed into his deepest fears about his own inadequacies. The perpetual threat that shadowed his every waking moment confirmed the thought he fought hardest to dismiss - that he was simply not the kind of person who could feel safe anymore. Feeling this perpetual threat led him to accept a painful truth: that he was now someone who could not feel safe, confirming his fears about his own weaknesses. This constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof Mark had that his life had changed beyond repair, reinforcing the belief that he could no longer navigate the world as he once did. He couldn't relax, even in the safety of his own home, where he would often find himself pacing the floor, trapped in a cycle of anxiety. The world around him felt perilous, and he had come to believe that danger lurked behind every corner. This heightened sense of threat fed into his deeply held negative beliefs about life. Feeling this afraid all the time, Mark had eventually come to accept the painful conclusion that he was not the kind of person who got to feel safe anymore, reinforcing his sense of worthlessness. Mark felt that nothing had any meaning anymore; the things that once brought him joy-the camaraderie of his colleagues, the satisfaction of his work-felt hollow and empty. The belief that he was permanently changed kept bringing him back to the moment of the earthquake, as if he needed to locate exactly where he had been lost in order to understand his current despair. Each time he replayed those memories, they only deepened his conviction that he was broken, as if this was the evidence of his failure to be the man he once believed himself to be. His conviction that he had failed to save lives that day made every recollection feel like a damning indictment of his worth, each memory a reminder of the man he believed he could no longer be. Each time he replayed that horrific day, the weight of his negative appraisals made the memories more vivid and accessible, as if they were waiting to validate his sense of failure. After each recollection surfaced, he would catch himself thinking that if he had been stronger, he could have saved more lives, solidifying the narrative of inadequacy that haunted him. Each time he replayed that horrific day, the memory reinforced his conviction that he was no longer the strong, dependable man he once was, further entrenching his sense of helplessness and despair. With each flashback, the thought that he had let his community down became more pronounced, leaving him with an overwhelming sense that he was fundamentally flawed and incapable. It seemed that every time he attempted to reconnect with the world, the memories of the earthquake would flood back, reinforcing his belief that he no longer knew who he was. 

As those memories surged, they twisted into a painful loop. Every time the memories of the earthquake flooded back, Mark found himself thinking that he had failed, deepening the belief that something was irrevocably wrong with him. Mark would recall the terror of that day, and in turn, he would feel a profound sense of loss over his previous self. The man who had once been confident and dependable was now a stranger, consumed by anguish and confusion. He couldn't shake the sense that his understanding of the world had been shattered, leaving him grappling with beliefs that felt like a distant memory. In moments of quiet, the weight of his thoughts bore down on him, pressing him into despair, as he struggled to make sense of a life that had spiraled into chaos. 

Despite the turmoil, Mark attempted to function. He returned to work as a medic, but his interactions had become strained. Colleagues noticed his withdrawn demeanor, and he often found himself avoiding social gatherings. The echoes of laughter and the sounds of life felt like a cruel reminder of what he had lost. He had started to isolate himself, believing that if he stayed away, he could avoid the overwhelming emotions that came with connection. Yet, this self-imposed solitude only deepened his feelings of identity loss; he felt further removed from who he had been before the earthquake. The more he pushed people away, the less he understood himself, caught in a cycle where each negative thought fed his memories of trauma, and those memories deepened his sense of hopelessness.

Finally, after months of wrestling with these unrelenting emotions, Mark found himself sitting in the waiting room of a mental health clinic. He had reached a breaking point-his life felt unmanageable, and he was terrified of what the future held. He hoped that this step might help him reclaim a sense of meaning or at least provide a way to process the trauma that had overtaken his life. What frightened him most was the thought of remaining trapped in this cycle forever, unable to make peace with the memories that haunted him or to find a way back to himself. In that moment of vulnerability, Mark felt a flicker of hope; perhaps, with guidance, he could begin to heal.
